summary: Venezuela is in northern South America, with the world's largest proven oil reserves and the world's highest waterfall, Angel Falls; in recent years it has gone through a severe economic and political crisis.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 16th century Spanish colonists founded towns along the Venezuelan coast, and Catholicism came with them; in the 17th and 18th centuries orders such as the Capuchins penetrated the plains and the Orinoco basin, founding mission villages among the indigenous peoples. According to tradition, in 1652 the Virgin appeared to an indigenous chief at Portuguesa, and "Our Lady of Coromoto" was later venerated as Venezuela's patroness. Although the government of Guzmán Blanco in the 19th century strongly weakened the church's power, Catholicism remains central to social and festive life and is still the largest religion today.

ranking.name: Protestantism / Evangelical
ranking.description: In the 19th century Protestantism arrived mainly with foreign merchants and immigrants, and its influence was limited. Since the 1970s Pentecostal and Evangelical churches have expanded rapidly in the poor neighborhoods of big cities, attracting followers with community mutual aid, faith healing and fervent worship; during the economic crisis and social turmoil of the 2010s, the support networks these churches provided attracted still more people, so their share has kept rising.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Those with no religion are concentrated mainly among young people and intellectuals in big cities such as Caracas, related to urbanization and the spread of education. In recent years the economic collapse has led millions of people to move abroad, and the demographic makeup of those remaining has also changed, but overall Venezuela is still a strongly religious society, and the share with no religion is not high.

religion.background: Venezuela's indigenous peoples originally had their own religious beliefs; after Spanish colonization in the 16th century Catholicism became the mainstream, and religious orders founded mission villages in the interior. After independence in the 19th century relations between government and church were tense, and in the 1870s the Guzmán Blanco government confiscated church property and pursued secularization. The oil economy of the 20th century brought immigration and urbanization, and Evangelicals grew rapidly after the 1970s. During the Chávez and Maduro periods the Catholic Church also became an important voice of criticism of the government.

language.official: Spanish is the official language, and the constitution also recognizes the official status of indigenous languages in indigenous regions.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish arrived with Spanish colonization in the early 16th century; Venezuelan Spanish belongs to the Caribbean dialect group, with a lively pronunciation that often drops the final "s." In 1847 the Caracas-born scholar Andrés Bello published his far-reaching Grammar of the Spanish Language, which set the standard for Spanish in the Americas. Because indigenous people, Africans and Europeans extensively intermixed and switched to Spanish during the colonial period, almost all citizens today speak Spanish as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Wayuu (Guajiro)
ranking.description: The Wayuu are Venezuela's most numerous indigenous people, living on the Guajira Peninsula and in Zulia State on the border with Colombia, traditionally making a living from herding and trade, and never fully conquered during the Spanish colonial period. Wayuunaiki belongs to the Arawakan family; the 1999 constitution recognized the official status of indigenous languages in their regions, and the 2008 Law on Indigenous Languages also promotes bilingual education.

language.history: Venezuela's indigenous languages belong to several families, including Cariban and Arawakan, and after colonization many languages disappeared or lost most of their speakers. From the 16th century Spanish became the main language, and in the 19th century the grammar written by Andrés Bello of Caracas influenced all of Latin America. The oil boom of the 20th century brought Italian, Portuguese and Spanish immigrants, and also added loanwords to Venezuelan Spanish. The 1999 constitution recognized the official status of indigenous languages for the first time.

ranking.name: Arepa
ranking.description: Corn flour is kneaded with water into round cakes, griddled or fried, then split open and stuffed with fillings such as cheese, black beans, chicken and avocado salad or shredded beef.
ranking.history: The history of the arepa goes back to the indigenous peoples before colonization, who ground maize into round cakes and cooked them on clay plates. In the past, making arepas required first boiling the corn and then laboriously grinding it; in the 1950s the engineer Luis Caballero Mejías invented pre-cooked corn flour, which went on sale under the "P.A.N." brand from 1960, making the arepa an everyday staple that anyone can make quickly. In recent years millions of Venezuelans have emigrated and opened arepa restaurants around the world.

ranking.name: Pabellón criollo
ranking.description: A plate holding shredded stewed beef, black beans, white rice and fried ripe plantain slices, sometimes with a fried egg added; it is the national dish of Venezuela.
ranking.history: This dish took shape gradually in the colonial period, combining the beef brought by the Spanish, the beans and plantains of African food traditions, and local rice and seasonings, and is regarded by many as a symbol of the blending of Venezuela's diverse peoples. "Pabellón" means "flag," and some believe that the many colors on the plate resemble the national flag. Today it is the most representative lunch in Venezuelan homes and restaurants.

ranking.name: Hallaca
ranking.description: Corn dough is filled with stewed beef, pork and chicken, with raisins, olives and capers added, then wrapped in banana leaves into a rectangle and boiled.
ranking.history: The hallaca is the representative food of Venezuelan Christmas and is generally believed to date from the colonial period, combining the indigenous corn cake, the Spanish olives and raisins and the African technique of wrapping in banana leaves. Folk tradition often says it originated with slaves wrapping the leftover ingredients from their masters' banquets in corn dough, but there are no definite historical records for this. Every December, the whole family, young and old, divide the work of making dozens or even hundreds of hallacas, and this family gathering is itself part of the festival.

ranking.name: Cachapa
ranking.description: A sweet batter ground from fresh corn kernels is fried on a griddle into a thick pancake, often folded over a soft fresh cheese, "queso de mano"; sweet and savory flavors mingle.
ranking.history: The cachapa method derives from the indigenous tradition of making food from fresh corn, and is sweeter and moister than the arepa, which uses dried cornmeal. It is closely linked with the cattle industry of the Venezuelan plains and central region, because the accompanying "queso de mano" is fresh cheese made on the ranches. Today cachapa stalls along the roadside are a classic scene on journeys in Venezuela.

ranking.name: Tequeños
ranking.description: Dough wrapped around sticks of white cheese is fried or baked, crisp outside and soft inside with stretching cheese, often dipped in guasacaca or other sauces.
ranking.history: The name tequeño is generally believed to come from the town of Los Teques near the capital, Caracas, where it is said to have become popular in the early 20th century before spreading across the country. It is an indispensable snack at Venezuelan birthday parties, weddings and all kinds of gatherings, and there is even a saying that "without tequeños it is not a party." In recent years, as Venezuelan emigrants have scattered around the world, tequeños have also become known abroad.
